description: Jeswanth, Ayaan, and Khush are talented software developers who consistently push past expected limits in competition. At FBLA Nationals, they placed in the top 10, and in an international drone competitions (SUAS), they ranked in the top 25 worldwide. Their combination of strong programming skills, hands-on engineering, and teamwork has earned them recognition against some of the best teams in the field.
summary: MoonMesh is a lunar communications planning tool designed for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It provides an overview of what areas can be contacted on Earth, when they will lose communications and how failures may affect communications. The user inputs their landing location (either Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, Malapert Massif or a custom drawn area) at the South Pole of the moon along with mission times. It uses NASA LOLA 20m topography and JPL DE440 SPICE ephemeris data to calculate the position of the sun and Earth relative to the true topography horizon at each time step. This results in a timeline of when there will be blackouts to Earth with an explanation of why they occur (topography, geometry or radio margin). It then filters through hundreds of potential relay locations. Surface relays are placed based on calculated line of sight coverage. Different network configurations can also be compared. Any relays can be turned off to see what connections remain. Different landing zones can also be compared side by side. During our test month at Haworth we saw adding relays increased our communication coverage from 48.0% to 60.9%. However, if one relay was lost our coverage dropped back down to 48.0%. This is the type of weakness we would want to identify before launch. All results include assumptions made and if requirements were met, failed or could not be proven.
details:
Overview

MoonMesh is designed to answer the simple question ‘will my astronaut be heard?’ by guiding you through 7 steps of planning your mission.

Explore.

View an interactive full screen 3D moon (CesiumJS) using NASA elevation data and LROC imagery. Fly to the NASA Artemis III candidate areas or any area on the map by adding a pin. Zoom in to get a 3D terrain view.

Set up.

Draw the area of your mission. Set the start & end date, sampling rate, and communication requirements such as minimum coverage, maximum allowable blackout, number of relays, budget and deployment radius.

Sites.

MoonMesh identifies suitable areas (565 areas at Haworth) within your mission region. It selects low and gentle areas for mines and areas with the longest Earth visibility for gateways. It selects relays and compares different topologies (tree, tree with loops and mesh) based on links, cable length, single points of failure and robustness.

Earth Coverage.

View the coverage over time between Direct to Earth and relay satellite. View the detailed 3D view of towers, links and orbiting relay satellite.

Blackouts.

View the timeline of your mission and how much of the mission has flat horizon visibility, Earth visibility, radio viability, sunlight, relay coverage and blackouts. Click on any blackouts to see a 360 view of your area showing the precise location of the Earth relative to the ridge line.

Robustness.

Turn off any relays and watch the coverage, blackout duration and alternative routes change instantly. The N−1 analysis will identify the worst single point of failure.

Cost.

Each node will be costed based on its role, longest link, distance travelled, slope, mast height and power sizing. An optional relay satellite can also be added. An itemised Excel file can be downloaded.

Additional Analysis Options.

Compare all landing areas during the same time period, perform sensitivity analysis, relay details, lunar night battery & thermal model, digital twin and underground mine network (ORA relay lab). Export results in JSON, CSV, Excel or printable format.

Science

Terrain.

Use high resolution NASA LRO LOLA polar data (20m near site, 240m up to 180km away). Rays are calculated to show Earth curvature and sampled in 2° increments up to 150km. Any missing terrain is noted and never counted as coverage.

Sun & Earth Positions.

JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 ephemeris, Lunar Mean Earth Frame) using the SpiceyPy library.

Radio.

Free space calculations (ITU-R P.525) for each hop with clear assumptions on the transmitter, antenna and margins.

Power & Thermal.

Every relay must be able to survive thermally & have power. The lander must also be able to survive. All missions are checked for the following scenarios: nominal, cold night, dust and cold with dust.

Relay Selection.

Suitable relay areas are identified by ranking them based on their visibility area calculation (8km). An exact greedy algorithm is used to select the best areas. All links are verified to have an exact line of sight.

Transparency.

All results have a status of Requirements met, Requirements failed or Insufficient Evidence. This shows what hazards have been checked and what have not. Prototype results will never be shown as guaranteed for flight.

Verification

Sun & Earth Positions.

Matches JPL Horizons data for 1452 samples for all 3 sites. An accuracy of 0.001° for elevation and 0.006° for azimuth.

Relay Coverage.

A high density line of sight check (73million rays) has been performed. This has a high correlation (R²=98.8%) and rank correlation (99.5%-99.6%). This was performed on unseen terrain.

Full Haworth Lander to Relay to Satellite to Earth simulation matches an independent 30 second reference. No discrepancies were found in 288 samples. Terrain clearance was validated using NASA PGDA 5m data.

Machine Learning

LightGBM models were trained from scratch:

Relay placement model was trained using real world data from 491 earth cell towers (FCC registry) on mountainous terrain.

Quick visibility calculator and relay selection model were trained using LOLA data. This achieves 94-96% of the exact greedy result.

Cold hazard model was trained using data from LRO Diviner polar temperatures.

All models were scored using sealed test windows. The app will never rely on these models to return results.

Benefits

South pole blackouts can be long due to the Earth setting behind crater edges. MoonMesh allows teams to visualise where blackouts happen, understand why they occur and try solutions such as placing relays, different sites or dates. Scenarios can be simulated to find failures early when changes are still low cost. This combines multiple analysis types into a single repeatable process.

Creativity

Relates each blackout to the terrain reason. Relays are related to how much they help coverage but also create risk if they fail.

Compared against real world networks on Earth. 11 Single Points of Failure were found using real world terrain vs 1 for an equivalent network with no terrain.

Cost model.

Digital Twin & underground mining extension use the same network engine.

Tools & Languages

Python 3.11+ (NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NetworkX, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Rasterio, pyproj, Numba, pandas, xarray, XlsxWriter, PyYAML, pytest)

TypeScript (CesiumJS, Three.js, esbuild)

Docker, Hugging Face Spaces, Vercel, GitHub Actions

No hardware.

Considerations

Scientific Integrity.

All assumptions have been labelled. Planning results will never be shown as guaranteed.

Terrain resolution.

Earth visibility vs Radio viability.

Thermal & power survival during Lunar Night.

Single Points of Failure.

User friendly for non specialist planner.

Satellite pass is just a quick view of the geometry. Main results will still be based on the direct to Earth baseline. These are planning results and are not flight qualified.
